title: Benchy: towards a universal language for task-oriented AI benchmarks
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

    Title:Benchy: towards a universal language for task-oriented AI benchmarks
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Benchy is a semantic language and execution engine for benchmarking AI programs. A benchmark is completely specified by a program, a scoring function, and a dataset, B=(P,S,D), and is separate from the AI-system taking it; a run binds the two, R=(B,AI). Benchmarks are authored as canonical YAML in which each semantic concept has one valid syntax, classified by a shared task/domain/language ontology, and deterministically compiled into a canonical JSON intermediate representation that the engine executes. Compilation changes representation, not meaning: it does not repair invalid definitions or inject hidden defaults. Programs use fixed schemas of named input and output fields, the leaf output fields are the scoring dimensions, and the engine exposes one universal runtime contract --- a named-field input object in, a named-field output object out --- to which external AI-systems adapt at the boundary, so integration mechanics never propagate into benchmark semantics. This paper gives the semantic object model, the ontology and task-to-program validation rule, the scoring and failure semantics, the compilation and execution architecture, and the scope of the current language. An appendix fixes the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation.

report.summary: Benchy proposes a YAML-based semantic language and execution engine to standardize task-oriented AI benchmarks, separating benchmark definitions from AI systems for reproducible evaluation.
report.background: AI benchmarking is fragmented. Teams use different harnesses, formats, scoring conventions, and dataset interfaces, making results hard to compare. Benchmark definitions are often entangled with model integration code, prompt wrappers, and hidden defaults, so changing an API can alter evaluation semantics. Task-oriented benchmarks for agents, tool use, and multi-step workflows amplify this problem. Existing suites such as HELM, lm-evaluation-harness, OpenAI Evals, and MLCommons help, but each has its own schema and assumptions. Benchy responds with a canonical YAML language, a shared task/domain/language ontology, a deterministic compiler to JSON intermediate representation, and an execution engine. It treats a benchmark as program, scoring function, and dataset, separate from the AI system, with a run binding the two. The goal is portable, versionable, cross-system comparability.
key_points: Benchmark as a formal object: Benchy defines a benchmark as B=(P,S,D) — program, scoring function, dataset — kept separate from the AI system. A run is R=(B,AI). This clean split means benchmark meaning does not change when you swap models, adapters, or integration code.

Canonical YAML and deterministic compilation: Authors write benchmarks in YAML with one valid syntax per semantic concept. The compiler deterministically lowers it to canonical JSON intermediate representation. It changes representation, not meaning: invalid definitions are not repaired, and hidden defaults are not injected. This supports auditability and reproducibility.

Shared task/domain/language ontology: Benchmarks are classified by an ontology and validated against task-to-program rules. Programs use fixed schemas of named input and output fields. Leaf output fields become scoring dimensions. This gives a common vocabulary for tasks, domains, languages, and metrics across benchmark authors.

Universal runtime contract: The engine exposes one interface — named-field input object in, named-field output object out. External AI systems adapt at the boundary. Integration mechanics such as APIs, SDKs, and prompt formats never propagate into benchmark semantics. This reduces per-model glue code and makes runs comparable across heterogeneous systems.

Scope and engineering contract: The paper gives the semantic object model, ontology, validation rule, scoring and failure semantics, compilation and execution architecture, and current language scope. An appendix fixes the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation, suggesting this is an early spec aimed at interoperability.

Model and agent vendors could publish once, run anywhere: If Benchy gains adoption, benchmark definitions could become portable artifacts that any compliant engine executes. That would improve comparability, make scoring semantics explicit, and reduce benchmark gaming through hidden prompts or custom glue code.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Benchy could push benchmarking toward declarative, portable specifications, similar to how containers standardized deployment or SQL standardized queries. Model and agent vendors could publish benchmark definitions that any compliant engine runs, improving comparability and reducing hidden assumptions. For developers, it promises less integration glue: adapt model I/O to one contract, reuse benchmarks across harnesses, and version definitions in Git. For regular users, better benchmarks mean clearer claims about assistant and agent reliability, though adoption will take time and depends on tooling, ontology coverage, and community buy-in. A key risk is becoming yet another standard if major evaluation suites do not adopt it.
report.tools: Watch Benchy's reference engine and specification once released. Related tools include EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness, Stanford HELM, OpenAI Evals, MLCommons MLPerf, Hugging Face Evaluate, and agent benchmark suites such as SWE-bench, GAIA, and AgentBench. YAML and JSON Schema validators, JSON IR tooling, and CI reproducibility tools like DVC or MLflow could help operationalize Benchy-style benchmarks.
